answer_text:
Let

\[
I(c)=\int_0^\infty \frac{dx}{(1+x^2)(1+x^c)},\qquad c\ge 0.
\]

First note the integral converges: near \(x=0\) the integrand is bounded, and as \(x\to\infty\),

\[
\frac{1}{(1+x^2)(1+x^c)}
\sim
\begin{cases}
\frac{1}{2x^2}, & c=0,\\[2mm]
\frac{1}{x^{c+2}}, & c>0,
\end{cases}
\]

so it is integrable.

Now use the inversion substitution \(x=\frac1t\). Then \(dx=-\frac{dt}{t^2}\), and the limits \(x:0\to\infty\) become \(t:\infty\to0\). Hence

\[
I(c)
=
\int_\infty^0
\frac{1}{\left(1+\frac1{t^2}\right)\left(1+\frac1{t^c}\right)}
\left(-\frac{dt}{t^2}\right).
\]

Reversing the limits gives

\[
I(c)
=
\int_0^\infty
\frac{1}{t^2}
\cdot
\frac{1}{\left(\frac{t^2+1}{t^2}\right)\left(\frac{t^c+1}{t^c}\right)}
\,dt.
\]

Simplifying,

\[
I(c)
=
\int_0^\infty
\frac{t^c}{(1+t^2)(1+t^c)}\,dt.
\]

Renaming \(t\) as \(x\),

\[
I(c)=\int_0^\infty \frac{x^c}{(1+x^2)(1+x^c)}\,dx.
\]

Now add this to the original expression for \(I(c)\):

\[
2I(c)
=
\int_0^\infty
\frac{1+x^c}{(1+x^2)(1+x^c)}\,dx
=
\int_0^\infty \frac{dx}{1+x^2}.
\]

The last integral is elementary:

\[
\int_0^\infty \frac{dx}{1+x^2}
=
\left[\arctan x\right]_0^\infty
=
\frac{\pi}{2}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
2I(c)=\frac{\pi}{2}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
I(c)=\frac{\pi}{4}.
\]

Thus for every \(c\ge 0\),

\[
\boxed{\frac{\pi}{4}}
\]
